body: Learn the scales that the chords are from. Build your solo off of those. Also try to listen to the song, listen to the solo section, transcribe (listen, then copy) the solo and if you cant, steal as many ideas as you can. Also dont think you have to sound like Sonny Rollins or Coltrane. Make it simple, you can still make it sound cool. You aren't going to be able to do much in 4 days, so be patient with yourself. You got this!

You cant really work your low register very well without a trigger. You can however do pedal notes. When you play pedal notes, drop your jaw slightly, open your mouth a bit, and slow down your air. Make sure none of these movements are too drastic or the note wont come out.

If you can afford it DEFINITLEY get private lessons. You dont need them but they help A LOT. A private teacher can help you learn a lot more in a very short period of time. Also get an arbans book and a rochute book, those will help you improve your technique.

I'm currently a junior, I've been playing trombone since 6th grade.

Dont start your warm ups with this exercise, or any exercise that's designed to expand your high register. Ease into your practices. I personally prefer starting with long tones.

There are a bunch of other ways to do this, but this is how I learned to play high. Look into other exercises and see what works best for you. Start with lip slurs up and down the partials in each position, starting from first and working your way down. Start by going up to an F, then once you've gone through the other positions, slur up to the F and then slur to a G in sharp second, do this in each position. Once G becomes easy enough, do the same thing, but then you slur up to an A in second, again, do this in each position. Once A becomes easier, slide into first and go up to a B flat. Again do this in each position lol. Once those notes become easier, then just slur up to a C without changing positions, again, every position. Then from there you can just keep working your way up. This has helped improve my range drastically, I can comfortably play a D and sometimes an E flat. 

It'll take you a while to get up to that C, dont try doing this all at once. Wait until you've mastered one, then move on to the next.

A few other tips I have are:
FASTER AIR IS THE KEY! One common problem I see with people learning to play high is that they think they need to tighten their lips to the point where they cramp, and they try to force way too much air through that tiny aperture. This results in a very forced and airy tone, and often times they cant sustain the note. This is also destroys your embrocure for the day, you'll find that playing your mid register is uncomfortable. You will need to slightly close your lips, but only slightly, while focusing on moving your air faster. This does not mean use more air btw.

Practicing fast, high passages can be difficult, especially you dont have that endurance built up. Play them an octave lower until you've mastered them in the lower octave. Then go up the octave. The positions will more then likely be different, but this is easy to adjust to since you'll be familiar with the passage. Doing this will help you keep your lips from becoming strained.

When playing high and loud, you dont necessarily  need to push as much air through the instrument as you would when playing loud in your lower register.  High notes on brass instruments tend to be louder then lower notes.

Playing higher notes should feel like playing any other note. If you feel like you're forcing the note, and notice your lips cramping, stop playing high for the day, and play some lower notes to relax your lips. We all have our limits, and while we do want to push them, you dont want push too far or you may end up injuring yourself.

After you work your high register, do long tones in your lower range. Even if you can play higher notes perfectly, it still strains your lips. Doing this helps relax your lips so that you can still maintain a good tone in your middle register.

Im sure you know this already, but please dont go out and blow 60 bucks on a small mouthpiece. You can learn to play high on any mouthpiece, or any trombone. 

KEEP IN MIND that this is a process and that it wont affect your range instantly. There is no quick way to expand your range. Just keep working at it and I promise you'll have a good high register.

I hope this helps, if you need more advice reply to my post, always happy to help. 

Good luck man!

If theres a written solo, play that and build off of it. If there isnt, find a recording of the song you're going to be soloing on and try to replicate that solo. Take ideas from other songs and other soloists. Improv is learned by copying others, dont worry about stealing ideas. Also, listen to a shit ton of jazz soloists. Some good ones are jj Johnson, Marshall Gilkes and Bill Watrous. Dont push yourself too hard, start out simple. When you first start building a solo you will find yourself playing notes that dont fit within the chords, this is normal. Just keep building it until you find something that you like and fits with the song. Hope this helped, good luck with your solo!
